en: Homage to the Buddha.
Having bowed with devotion to the five Buddhas and the Yoginīs as well,
I shall explain the Fivefold Aspect for my own recollection.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure by nature; I am pure by nature.
Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Vajrasattva is the drop (bindu); Vairocana is considered to be the half-moon;
the line belongs to the Lord of Jewels (Ratneśa), and the syllable HA is said to be Amitābha.
The syllable Oṃ is Amoghasiddhi; indeed, the world consists of the nature of the five Buddhas.

In the east is Vairocana, white in color, marked by the wheel, the aggregate of form, of the Jewel family, the Great Chinese Tradition, the purification of the mind, possessing mirror-like wisdom, receiving the vajra initiation, having a solar mandala, and displaying the boon-granting mudrā; his seed-syllable is Aṃ.

In the south is Ratnasaṃbhava. He is yellow in color, has the jewel as his emblem, is the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), belongs to the Jewel family (ratna-kula), is seated upon a solar disc, possesses the wisdom of equality (samatā-jñāna), and holds the boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā). His seed-syllable is TRĀṂ. In the west is Amitābha. He is red in color, has the lotus as his emblem, is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), represents the stage of generation (utpatti-krama), is the purification of passion (rāga-viśuddhi), possesses the wisdom of discernment (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna), is consecrated by the Vajra, is seated upon a solar disc, and is endowed with the meditative concentration gesture (samādhi-mudrā). His seed-syllable is HRĪṂ.

In the north is Amoghasiddhi; green in color, with a sword as his emblem, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) as his body, belonging to the Karma family, with the stride of the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*), the purification of envy, the gnosis of all-accomplishing action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), consecrated by the bell, seated upon a solar disc, endowed with the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*), and his seed-syllable is *khaṃ*.

In the center is Akṣobhya: black in color, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), following the sequence of Cakrasattva, purified of hatred, the gnosis of the perfectly pure dharmadhātu, the water initiation, possessing a solar mandala, and endowed with the earth-touching mudrā; his seed-syllable is *hūṃ*.
Now the colors and symbols of the yoginīs are described:

In the direction of fire (the southeast) is Locanā. She is white in color, has the nature of the earth element, is purified of delusion, is born from the Tathāgata family, and dwells in loving-kindness (*maitrī*). She holds a wheel in her left hand and displays the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) in her right; she is seated upon a moon mandala. Her seed-syllable is *lāṃ*. *Oṃ ........... jvala tiṣṭha siddha māraṇi sarvārthasādhani mama śāntiṃ kuru svāhā.*

In the southwest is the goddess Māmakī. She is black in color, whose nature is the water element, purified of hatred, born of the Vajra family, and dwelling in compassion. She holds a vajra in her left hand and displays the boon-granting gesture in her right; she is seated upon a moon mandala. Her seed-syllable is *māṃ*. *Oṃ saṃskāraśāntikare ghuṭa ghuṭa ghuṭinī ghoṭaya ghoṭaya ghuṭinī...* [svāhā].

In the northwest is Pāṇḍarā. She is red in color, has the nature of the fire element, is pure in speech, and is born from the family of Amitābha. [She dwells in joy. She holds a lotus symbol in her left hand and displays the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) in her right; she is seated upon a moon mandala. Her seed-syllable is *pāṃ*. Oṃ kaṭa vikaṭa nikaṭa kaṣṭaṃ kara kapāṭa svāhā.

In the northeast is Tāraṇī (or Tāriṇī). She is green in color, whose nature is the wind element; she is the purification of envy, born from the family of Amoghasiddhi, and dwells in equanimity. She holds a blue lotus in her left hand and displays the gesture of granting boons with her right; she is seated upon a moon mandala. Her seed syllable is *tāṃ*. Oṃ tāre tuttāre [ture] svāhā.

In the center is Vajradhātvīśvarī. She is the color of the sky, has the nature of the sky, is born from the Ratnasambhava family, and possesses a solar disc. She holds a lotus in her left hand and a five-pronged vajra—the symbol of the *dharmadhātu*—in her [other] left; she grants boons with her right hand. Her seed-syllable is *dhāṃ*. *Oṃ prajñe mahāprajñe śrutismṛtivijaye dhīḥ svāhā.* Feces is Vairocana; urine is Akṣobhya; blood is Ratnasambhava; semen is Amitābha; and flesh is Amoghasiddhi.

Regarding the elements of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena: in form is Vairocana; in sound, Akṣobhya; in smell, Ratnasaṃbhava; in taste, Amitābha; in the body, Amoghasiddhi; and in the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu), Vajrasattva.

Regarding the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: in the two eyes is Vairocana; in the two ears, Akṣobhya; in the nose, Ratnasaṃbhava; in the tongue, Amitābha; in the body, Amoghasiddhi; and in the mind, Vajrasattva.

In eye-consciousness is Rūpavajrā; in ear-consciousness is Śabdavajrā; in nose-consciousness is Gandhavajrā; in tongue-consciousness is Rasavajrā; in body-consciousness is Sparśavajrā; and in mind-consciousness is Dharmadhātuvajrā.

The ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) is now described: the eye is placed in *oṃ*, the ear in *hūṃ*, the nose in *ḍāṃ*, the tongue in *hrīṃ*, the body in *khaṃ*, and the head in *vaṃ*. Kṣitigarbha is in the two eyes, Vajrapāṇi in the two ears, Khagarbha in the two nostrils, Lokeśvara on the tongue, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin in the body, and Samantabhadra in the mind. To the east is Yamāntaka; he is black in color, mounted upon a buffalo, holding a vajra and a goad in his hands, embraced by Vajraḍākinī, and seated upon a solar disc. His seed-syllable is *hūṃ*.

In the south is Prajñāntaka; white in color, mounted upon a lion, holding a vajra-noose in his hand, embraced by Vajranakhī, possessing a solar disc, and his seed-syllable is HŪṂ. In the west is Padmāntaka; red in color, mounted upon a tiger, holding a vajra-bell in his hand, embraced by Aparājitā, possessing a solar disc, and his seed-syllable is HŪṂ.
These four wrathful deities (krodhas) are the purifications of the four Tathāgatas.

Now the elements (*dhātu*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are explained: Earth is solid; its function is to provide support through stability. The earth element consists of bone, intestine, sinew, tooth, skin, hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth. The water element is liquid; its function is cohesion. It includes pond water, river water, phlegm, nasal mucus, tears, urine, and so forth.

The fire element (*tejodhātu*) consists of heat in the navel, heat in the heart, heat in all limbs, drying up, the state of being hot, the drying of karma, ripening, and lightness; this is the fire element.

The wind element (*vāyudhātu*) consists of contraction, expansion, going and coming, exhalation, inhalation, upward movement, downward movement, carrying away, bringing together, the *kūrma* [wind], the *kṛkara* [wind], the *naradatta* [wind], the *dhanañjaya* [wind], and so forth.

How is the space-element (ākāśadhātu) pervasive within emptiness regarding the grasped, the grasper, and so forth? These belong to the yogins and the Tathāgatas. The elixir (rasāyana) is explained as follows: Akṣobhya is in the bitter; Vairocana in the sweet; Ratnasaṃbhava in the salty; Amitābha in the sour; Amoghasiddhi in the pungent; and Vajrasattva in the astringent. Vairocana is in the *ka*-group; Akṣobhya in the *ca*-group; Ratnasaṃbhava in the *ṭa*-group; Amitābha in the *ta*-group; Amoghasiddhi in the *pa*-group; and Vajrasattva in the *ya*-group. These are the consonants (*vyañjana*).

A Ā I Ī U Ū Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ E AI O AU AṂ AḤ—these vowels are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the goddesses. The letter *A* and so forth are wisdom (*prajñā*). Vairocana should be sealed by Akṣobhya; Akṣobhya should be sealed by Vajrasattva. By what is Vajrasattva sealed? According to the principle of father and son, Akṣobhya is not sealed; for among the other Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya alone is the leader.

The division of days is explained as follows: at dawn Vairocana; at midday Akṣobhya; during the third watch Ratnasaṃbhava; in the afternoon Amitābha; at midnight Amoghasiddhi; and from the third watch until dawn Vajrasattva. During the day Vajrasattva, and at night Prajñā.
In autumn Akṣobhya; in winter Vairocana; in the rainy season Ratnasaṃbhava; in spring Amitābha; in summer Amoghasiddhi; and in the cold season Vajrasattva.
In the *dharmadhātu* there is Vajrasattva; in gnosis there is Vajrasattva; in the mind there is Vajrasattva; throughout the entire triple world, the single-purpose Vajrasattva is praised.
The entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, consists of the five aspects.
Even though this world is seen as being without external conceptual construction, [it is not so].
The five Buddhas are proclaimed by way of the intrinsic nature of the five aggregates;
liberated from the five obscurations, they are the five Kaulikas residing within the aggregates.
What are the five obscurations to be known? Affliction, birth, and karma, as well as knowledge and ignorance—
these are the five obscurations taught by the Tathāgatas.
Reflecting thus, the wise one should constantly cultivate this;
he attains the foremost enlightenment spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One.
Thus ends the *Pañcākārābhisambodhi*.
